items.prompt: Which part of the eye captures light and sends signals to the brain?

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: The lens focuses light, but it does not capture it or send signals. The retina is the layer that catches light and starts the signal to the brain.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: Correct. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, full of cells that turn light into nerve signals for the brain.

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: The pupil is just the opening that lets light in, not a part that captures it. The capture happens deeper inside, on the retina.

options.label: The iris
options.feedback: The iris is the coloured ring that controls the pupil's size. Light is not captured there; it passes through the pupil to the retina.

items.ok_line: The retina is the eye's light-catching layer.
items.ko_line: Lens, pupil, and iris manage light but do not catch it.
items.exp_text: Light enters through the pupil, is focused by the lens, and lands on the retina. The retina is where the actual capture happens: its cells convert light into electrical signals sent along the optic nerve to the brain. Night animals often have a retina packed with rod cells to catch even tiny amounts of light.

items.prompt: What are the tiny light-sensitive cells in the retina called?

options.label: Nerves
options.feedback: Nerves carry signals, but the cells that directly sense light are special cells called photoreceptors. Nerves come after them in the pathway to the brain.

options.label: Pupils
options.feedback: The pupil is an opening in the iris, not a cell. The sensing cells sit in the retina, far behind the pupil.

options.label: Photoreceptors
options.feedback: Correct. Photoreceptors are the retina's special cells — rods and cones — that absorb light and turn it into signals. They are the first step in seeing.

options.label: Lenses
options.feedback: The lens is a transparent structure that bends light, not a sensing cell. The cells that sense light are inside the retina.

items.ok_line: These cells catch light and start vision.
items.ko_line: Nerves, pupils, and lenses are not the sensing cells.
items.exp_text: Photoreceptors are found in the retina, and there are two kinds: rods and cones. Rods work in dim light and see in black and white; cones work in bright light and see colour. Night animals usually have many more rods than cones, which lets them see well when it is dark.

items.prompt: What is the coloured ring around the pupil called?

options.label: The iris
options.feedback: Correct. The iris is the coloured muscle ring that surrounds the pupil and changes its size to control how much light enters the eye.

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: The sclera is the white outer coat of the eye that protects it. The coloured part you see around the pupil is the iris, not the sclera.

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is the clear front window of the eye that bends light. It is not coloured and does not surround the pupil like a ring.

options.label: The optic nerve
options.feedback: The optic nerve is a cable behind the eye that carries signals to the brain. It is deep inside, not the coloured ring around the pupil.

items.ok_line: The iris is the coloured ring that opens and closes the pupil.
items.ko_line: Sclera, cornea, and optic nerve are different structures.
items.exp_text: The iris is a ring of muscle with colour in it. By relaxing or tightening, it makes the pupil bigger in the dark and smaller in bright light. In night animals like cats, the iris can open the pupil very wide to let in more light, and in bright light it can narrow it to a thin slit.

items.prompt: Which part of the eye focuses light onto the retina?

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: The pupil is just an opening; it does not bend light. The lens behind it does the focusing.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is where light lands, not where it is focused. The focusing happens before light reaches it.

options.label: The iris
options.feedback: The iris only changes the size of the pupil. It does not focus light; the lens shapes the light beam.

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: Correct. The lens is a transparent, flexible disc that bends incoming light to bring it into sharp focus on the retina. Its shape can change to focus near or far objects.

items.ok_line: The lens bends light to form a clear image on the retina.
items.ko_line: Pupil, iris, and retina do not focus light.
items.exp_text: Light enters through the cornea, then passes through the lens, which bends it to meet exactly on the retina. The lens can change its curvature to focus on objects at different distances. Without it, the image would blur like a photo out of focus.

items.prompt: What is the clear front part of the eye called?

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is at the back of the eye, not the front. The clear front part is the cornea.

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: Correct. The cornea is the transparent dome at the very front of the eye. It lets light in and starts bending it toward the lens.

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: The lens is inside the eye, behind the iris, not at the front surface. The clear front cover is the cornea.

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: The sclera is the tough white outer layer, not clear. The transparent front window is the cornea.

items.ok_line: The cornea is the clear dome that starts focusing light.
items.ko_title: Not the back or the white
items.ko_line: Retina, lens, and sclera are not the front clear part.
items.exp_text: The cornea is the curved, transparent layer at the front of the eye. It is the first surface light hits, and it does about two-thirds of the focusing before the lens fine-tunes it. Because it is clear, you can see the iris and pupil behind it.

items.prompt: What is the opening in the centre of the iris called?

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: The lens is a solid, curved structure behind the iris. The opening in the iris is the pupil.

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is the outer clear layer, not an opening. The hole in the middle of the iris is the pupil.

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: Correct. The pupil is the black circle in the middle of the iris. Light enters the eye through this opening.

options.label: The optic disc
options.feedback: The optic disc is where the optic nerve leaves the retina, deep inside the eye. It is not an opening at the front.

items.ok_line: The pupil is the black opening that lets light into the eye.
items.ko_title: Not the clear or solid parts
items.ko_line: Lens, cornea, and optic disc are not the iris's opening.
items.exp_text: The pupil looks black because light that enters goes inside and is absorbed. The iris surrounds it and changes its size. In dim light the pupil enlarges to let more light in; in bright light it shrinks to protect the retina from too much.

items.prompt: Which type of photoreceptor works best in very dim light?

options.label: Rod cells
options.feedback: Correct. Rod cells are extremely sensitive to low light levels, so they let animals see at night, though only in shades of grey.

options.label: Cone cells
options.feedback: Cone cells need bright light to work well and are for colour vision. They are nearly useless in the dark.

options.label: Ganglion cells
options.feedback: Ganglion cells are nerve cells that carry signals from the retina to the brain, not photoreceptors that sense dim light.

options.label: Horizontal cells
options.feedback: Horizontal cells connect other retinal cells to refine signals, but they do not detect light. Rods are the dim-light sensors.

items.ok_line: Rod cells are the retina's dim-light specialists.
items.ko_line: Colour-sensing cones cannot work in low light.
items.exp_text: Rods contain a pigment that reacts to even a single photon of light, making them perfect for night vision. That is why nocturnal animals have retinas packed with rods. However, rods cannot tell colours apart, so night vision is black and white.

items.prompt: Which type of photoreceptor gives colour vision?

options.label: Rod cells
options.feedback: Rod cells only sense light levels, not colours. They give black-and-white vision in dim light. Cone cells are the colour ones.

options.label: Bipolar cells
options.feedback: Bipolar cells pass signals from photoreceptors to other cells; they are not light-sensitive themselves. Cone cells detect colour.

options.label: Amacrine cells
options.feedback: Amacrine cells are interneurons in the retina that help process signals, not detect colour. Cone cells do that job.

options.label: Cone cells
options.feedback: Correct. Cone cells respond to different wavelengths of light — red, green, or blue — and the brain combines their signals to see colours. They need bright light to work.

items.ok_line: Cone cells are the retina's colour sensors.
items.ko_line: Rods, bipolar, and amacrine cells do not give colour.
items.exp_text: Cone cells come in three types, each sensitive to a different colour of light. In bright conditions they fire strongly, giving a colourful picture. Many night animals have few cones, which is why they see the night world mostly in shades of grey and blue.

items.prompt: What is the tough white outer layer of the eye called?

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is the clear front part, not white or tough over the whole eye. The white outer coat is the sclera.

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: Correct. The sclera is the strong, white, fibrous layer that covers most of the eye, protecting its inner structures and giving the eye its shape.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is the inner light-sensitive layer, not the outer coat. The white outer layer is the sclera.

options.label: The choroid
options.feedback: The choroid is a dark layer between the sclera and retina that supplies blood. It is not the white outer shell.

items.ok_line: The sclera is the eye's tough white outer shell.
items.ko_line: Cornea, retina, and choroid are not the white coat.
items.exp_text: The sclera is made of tough connective tissue and covers about five-sixths of the eye's surface. It keeps the eye's shape and protects the delicate retina inside. The front sixth is the clear cornea, which is continuous with the sclera but transparent.

items.prompt: Where is the blind spot located in the eye?

options.label: In the centre of the lens
options.feedback: The lens is clear and lets all light through, so it has no blind spot. The blind spot is on the retina.

options.label: In the middle of the pupil
options.feedback: The pupil is an opening that lets light pass, so it cannot be blind. The blind spot is in the retina.

options.label: Where the optic nerve leaves the retina
options.feedback: Correct. At the optic disc, where the optic nerve exits, there are no photoreceptors, so that spot cannot detect light — creating a blind spot in vision.

options.label: At the edge of the cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is clear and has no blind spot; it lets light through everywhere. The blind spot is inside, on the retina.

items.ok_line: The spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina has no photoreceptors.
items.ko_line: Lens, pupil, and cornea are not the blind spot.
items.exp_text: At the optic disc, nerve fibres from the retina gather to form the optic nerve and leave the eye. This area is packed with nerve cells but has no rods or cones, so light hitting it produces no signal. The brain fills in the gap, so we usually do not notice it.
